June 11 by the Ore and Coal Exchange of Cleveland of said embargo in view of the Canadian lake shipping strike.
This is a very grave emergency, as grave as in 1917. A year ago we had a coal pile of
800,000	tons in the ship channel in my constituency. On Sunday I visited it and it was down to 10,000 or 12,000 tons, and the coal piles of other municipalities are down in about the same proportion.
I understand that the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) is away today. I do not wish to interfere with the business of the house, but perhaps I might be allowed to speak for three or four minutes.
I	am doubtful, however, whether in that case the discussion could be revived to-morrow because of standing order 31 (6) (c). But as there is a grave national emergency, the worst in our history, I suggest that I might be allowed to speak for a few minutes.

II	by the Ore and Coal Exchange of Cleveland of said embargo in view of the Canadian lake shipping strike.
I wish to make a comment, for the benefit of the house more especially, on one point made by the hon. gentleman on the question of urgency. Urgency within the meaning of the rule is not a question whether a matter proposed to be discussed is of urgent importance. It may be of infinitely urgent importance to those affected. The question is whether it is urgent within the meaning of citation 239, Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms; in other words whether it is a matter of such urgency that harm would be caused to the public interest if by the ordinary opportunity provided by the rules of the house an hon. member were not able to bring the subject before the house soon enough. In the present case I am of the opinion that there is no urgency to adjourn the house today to discuss the subject, because the minister of the department concerned is not in the house this afternoon. Consequently I would rule the motion of the hon. gentleman out of order.

speechtext:
I shall not read subsection 3; it merely says that if the fraction is less than one-half, it is not counted; if it is more than one-half, it is counted as a whole number.
Subsection 4 is the one which we have to interpret; it reads as follows:
(4) On any such readjustment the number of members for a province shall not be reduced unless the proportion which the number of the population of the province bore to the number of the aggregate population of Canada at the then last preceding readjustment of the number of members for the province is ascertained at the then latest census to be diminished by one-twentieth part or upwards.
I submit that this subsection means that there shall not 'be any reduction in the representation of any province unless the fraction representing its quota of the population of Canada is reduced by five per cent. Let me take an example. Let us assume that in 1931 the population of this dominion was ten millions. Let us assume that the population of British Columbia was three millions. The proportion of the population of British Columbia would be thirty per cent. It would have thirty per cent of the population of the dominion; and if on that proportion it had twenty members it would hold those twenty members until when?- until that thirty per cent was reduced by five per cent. Five per cent of thirty per cent is one and a half per cent; therefore the representation of British Columbia in this house would remain at twenty members until its proportion of the population was reduced to 28} per cent. That is the meaning of this section. I submit that it can mean nothing else. People have wondered why it was inserted. The reason for which it was inserted is clear to me. The reason was that it was not the intent, it was not the desire, of the fathers of confederation that changes should be made in representation every time that there was the slighetest shift in population. The fathers of confederation said that once an allotment of a specific number of members had been made to a province it should keep that number until there was a substantial change in the proportion or the fraction of the whole population of Canada represented by the population of the province in question. That is simple; it is reasonable, it seems to me almost beyond dispute.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
I am prone to agree with almost any proposition of law that may be advanced by the right hon. gentleman, but I am going to say to him, with the greatest respect, that I shall deal with that particular problem in a moment. At present I should like to read the French text. Subsection 4 of section 51 of the French text is in these terms:
(Translation):
On any such readjustment the number of members for a province shall not be reduced . . .
On any such readjustment the number of members for a province shall not be reduced unless the proportion which the number of the population of the province bore to the number of the aggregate population of Canada at the then last preceding readjustment of the number of members for the province is ascertained at the then latest census to be diminished by one-twentieth part or upwards:
(Text): There we have it thrown into even bolder relief that what determines the right of a province to more members, or what determines the right of other provinces to see a

Redistribution
certain province reduced in membership, is a comparison. There is no dispute that one side of the comparison is the last census, that of 1941; but how far back must we go? Here I come to the question put to me a moment ago by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). You go back as far as it is necessary to go to get to the point where, to use the French expression, "lors de l'attribution precedente des sieges a la province" and in the English version, "to the last preceding readjustment of the number of members for the province." I submit that you must go back to the last time the members were reallocated to the province; not to the last census but to the time the twenty members were allocated to British Columbia, in the example I gave a few minutes ago. Let us assume that British Columbia had twenty members assigned to it by the census of 1911; and again to answer the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, let us assume that British Columbia had lost one and a half per cent in one decennial period and two and a half per cent in another decennial period, and that finally in the third it lost a fraction sufficient to make the total five per cent. Then in my submission the fourth subsection of section 61 of the act would come into play and the reduction in number of members must follow.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: Has it worked that way in case of Ontario?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
It has not worked that way, and that is just my complaint. A few moments ago I said I considered that the sub-section is beyond criticism. I wish I could say as much of those who had to do with its operation. I submit that the act itself provides for representation by population, with certain exceptions which we are not discussing at the moment; I say to the minister that under the act this house should be reduced to 230 members, and that this may be done by observing the text of section 51, without amending it in any respect whatsoever. The minister has put on record the number of members who would be allotted to the different provinces if the act were followed, but I do not agree with him when he gives the province of Ontario 82 members. It is my suggestion that the province of Ontario is entitled only to 74 members; and again to answer the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, it was entitled to 74 members and no more at the last redistribution.
Here someone may say to me, "Well, you were in the house at that time. What did you do about it?" I was in the house; like 63260-154
the majority of those who sit opposite I sat on a back bench, and I had just about as much to do with the policies of the country as they have at the present time. Now let me say this. I have read the debates carefully. Eight Hon. Mr. Bennett spoke of a reduction of one-twentieth in population as being the requisite to the application of subsection 4. Mr. King sat opposite, and he was much more concerned in working parishes and townships into electoral divisions and matters of that kind than with the principle of readjustment of the number of members among provinces. Mr. King acquiesced. That good and honourable gentleman who has gone to his reward, Right Hon. Mr. Lapointe, said, "I wonder why this subsection 4 was put in. I can find no reason for it. I think it should be deleted." At that time nobody referred to the Prince Edward Island case, which I am going to discuss. Possibly it required the deep knowledge of the law and the intimate acquaintance with, the decisions of the privy council which is possessed by the right hon. Minister of Justice to bring that to the assistance of his government; but at no time until he came on the horizon was it mentioned. In November, 1932, they seem to have proceeded on the basis that because the province of Ontario had not. lost five per cent of its population, this subsection did not apply.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext: They proceeded on the assumption that Ontario had not lost that percentage in the ten-year period.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Yes, and that was all they considered; the ten-year period. I went to the trouble of looking up the bill. In those days bills contained a great deal of information on the fly-leaf. There I found set out the article of the British North America Act and a great deal of other information. Nothing was said about the Prince Edward Island judgment, but I do find on turning to the census of Canada, volume 2, at page 3, that in 1911 the proportion of the population of Ontario to the whole population of Canada was 35-07.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The second volume of which census?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
The census of 1941. The representation of Ontario in this house could not be reduced under the section of the act I have read, unless that proportion or percentage of 35-07 per cent was reduced by one-twentieth, or five per cent. If one takes his pencil in hand, he will find that five per cent of 35-07 per cent, which was the fraction of Canada's population which represented the population of Ontario in 1911, amounts to 1-75

Redistribution

per cent. If he subtracts 1-75 per cent from 35-07 per cent he will find that the fraction is 33-31 per cent, and that Ontario was entitled to eighty-two members until the proportion of its population was reduced to 33-31 per cent. In 1931, according to the same book and the same page, it was reduced to 33-07 per cent. At that time the representation of Ontario in the house should have been reduced. It should be reduced to-day, under the terms of the act, unless we are going to say that there is something which limits the computation to the ten-year period between censuses.
Here I must tell the house how amazed I was when reading this bulletin No. A.IOput out by the Department of Trade and Commerce, which cites verbatim section 51 of the British North America Act and its subsections in the English text, to find in the French text in the place of subsection 4 I have just read, the following:
(Translation):
(4) On'any readjustment the number of members for a province shall not be reduced unless the proportion which the population of that province bore to the aggregate population of the dominion has diminished by at least one-twentieth part from one census to the next.
(Text): That is an entire perversion of the sense of subsection 4 of section 51; and not only is it a perversion but it is a denial of its sense and meaning. It is a substitution of the word "census" for the word "readjustment," or in the French language, the words, attribution de la 'population.
I should like to add another word in support of the interpretation I have put forth. I know this probably is not the place where one might hope to make a protracted legal argument. But I submit to the house that unless the interpretation I have given to these words is the real interpretation, then the words found in the third to the last line of subsection 4 are entirely superfluous; they are:
On any such readjustment the number of members for a province shall not be reduced unless the proportion which the number of the population of the province bore to the number of the aggregate population of Canada at the then last preceding-
Not census, but-
-readjustment of the number of members for the province is ascertained-
And so on. If we were to interpret this act, as it is being interpreted for the purpose of this redistribution, the words "of the number of members for the province" would be entirely superfluous, because they add nothing to the sense of the sentence, and the same result would be achieved without them.

I want to say one further word about the interpretation. With the exception of section 51A enacted to protect the maritime province0, by the amendment of 1915, the fundamental theory of this section is representation by population. Any interpretation of this subsection which would exact the loss of one-twentieth of the population between two succeeding censuses would be a complete denial of the theory of representation by population. As suggested by the hon. member from Winnipeg, it would mean that a province could lose 4-99 per cent of its proportion or percentage in one ten-year period, and the same in the next ten-year period, and the same in the next, until a period was reached where there might not be enough population in a province to supply the members to which it would be entitled under the section.

speechtext:
Well, one may laugh if he wishes. But I have not been critical of men on the other side of the house when they have made misstatements and when they have taken positions which they have had to abandon within a few minutes, because I knew that they were overburdened with work, that they were harrassed by strikes and troubles and endless worries. I submit that is a possible explanation for what happened in 1932 so far as the leader of the government is concerned. I should have to stretch my imagination a little further to find an excuse for the seeming negligence of the leader of the opposition and those who sat beside him at that time.
In 1905 the privy council handed down a judgment in the Prince Edward Island case. People from that province, and from Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, felt that the act was working a hardship on them; their grievances were heard on reference to the supreme court of Canada. Prince Edward Island submitted this question to the supreme court- and just listen to it:
Although the population of Prince Edward Island as ascertained at the census of 1901 if divided by the unit of representation ascertained by dividing the number of 65 into the population of Quebec is not sufficient to give six members

Redistribution
in the House of Commons of Canada to that province, is the representation of Prince Edward Island in the House of Commons of Canada liable under the British North America Act, 1867, and amendments thereto, and the terms of union of 1873, under which that province entered confederation to be reduced below six, the number granted to that province by the said terms of union of 1873?
The supreme court answered in the affirmative, and said that its representation must be reduced below six. The. privy council answered the same way. Its answer is found in just a word. The privy council found that it was stipulated that the representation of Prince Edward Island in confederation would be determined by the act and by the section I have read. Then the privy council went on to say m what I call an obiter dictum-not something which had any bearing on the question, not something which was necessary for its decisions, not something which had been submitted, although there had been a reference to it when a judge of the supreme court had asked a question and Mr. Newcombe had answered it but the question had never been raised as an issue, so the statement of the bench is purely an obiter dictum which was never argued and is not a binding authority:
This argument assumes that there has been no readjustment for any province unless there has been alteration. Their Lordships think this is to give too narrow a meaning to the word. In their opinion, when as a result of a census the representation of the provinces is reconsidered and the necessary changes, if any, made to bring it into harmony with the results of the census, that is a readjustment within the meaning of subsection 4, whether there be or be not any change in the case of any particular province. Their Lordships, therefore, think that the answer of the supreme court to the question submitted to it was correct.
That is an obiter dictum. It has no bearing on the case then at issue. It was not argued. Mr. Newcombe did say in the supreme court that he considered that the count to determine if the proportion had been reduced began every ten years.
We are not here dealing with petty matters. We are dealing with the most sacred thing we have in our national life, our constitution, and are we going to amend it without some serious reason? We have before us an agency which enables us to effect redistribution and deal fairly with each province of the dominion. I have an idea that this motion is just another phase of the old feud between the provinces and the dominion, and that the dominion is seeking to exact by promises, by gold, and by favours of different kinds, the assent of the provinces to the proposition that the British North America Act may be amended by the mere whim, by the smallest 63260-1541
majority of a political party in the two houses of parliament. I say, Mr. Speaker, that such practice, if tolerated, is prejudicial to parliament; it is prejudicial to our national life. It is in my estimation the first note of the requiem of confederation.
There may be another reason for introducing this act. It may be to save the face of those who were asleep at the switch in 1932. The government may now seek to make it appear that the amendment is necessary to go behind the census of 1931, to warrant a reallocation of seats to the provinces. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that there is no reason to amend the British North America Act. Its terms are explicit; they are clear. I admit that an advocate and a great advocate, in the supreme court, taken by surprise, did answer a question in a way which might be construed as contrary to the view that I have expressed here. The statement in the P-E.I. case was an obiter dictum of the privy council in a case where this question was not argued and where it was not in issue and where it has not authority.
I ask is there a reason for us, we here in adult Canada, to seek an amendment to our constitution when there is no provision for amending the act? The other day when we wanted to amend the act to incorporate in section 91 the subject of unemployment insurance we went to each of the provinces and got them to acquiesce. Oh, it may be said, but that was a provincial matter. The people of this country, peoples and nations, do not deal in subtleties of that kind. If there is a right in parliament alone to have the constitution amended, there will always be those who are clever enough and subtle enough to make a good case for the amendment, whether it affects provincial or national issues. I agree with what was said last night on the point by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Picard). No means have been provided to amend this act, and until those means are found we must in the interval proceed warily. The only way in which the act can be amended decently and properly is with the consent of the high contracting parties, the dominion and the provinces.
My hon. friend the member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) argued the case in the house the other day and put on the record the statements of every great constitutional lawyer. I would mention just two or three of them. There was Doherty; there was Borden; there was Blake; there was Meighen; there was Laurier; there was Lapointe-and not one of them said that this act could be altered without the consent of the provinces
Redistribution

and it should not be altered now without their consent for purposes which appear to be highly strategic.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am taking part in this debate because I realize the full import of the resolution now before us. First may I congratulate the right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) upon his masterly presentation of the redistribution resolution on the 28th of last month. If I read public opinion aright, from the press and the opinions of my own constituents, this resolution has been wonderfully received by almost every section of our population. It deals with an important problem. So far as I am concerned I strongly support the resolution.
I listened attentively to the learned address made by the previous speaker, the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett), and as I listened to him my conviction strengthened that our redistribution arrangements should be changed. It would be impossible, I should think, for any member to explain in a way that would be grasped clearly by most of our people what was meant by subsection 4 of section 51 of the British North America Act. No one can challenge or be against representation by population. It is a primary principle which has been adopted by all nations that call themselves democracies. It is the only just and fair way to decide the number of our representatives.
The previous speaker mentioned that Ontario under the present system had more members than she was entitled to for at least ten years. But let us take the 65 members assigned to the province of Quebec, and suppose that twenty years from now the population is 20,000,000 people, If Quebec then has a population of 6,000,000 the unit of representation will be 92,300 people per riding. That would give the rest of Canada 152 members, or a total for the whole country of 217 members, and that process would be accentuated as time goes on and our population grows. The present method of representation by population, dividing the population of the province of Quebec by 65 to give the unit of representation, has worked fairly well up to the present, but it will not work in the future, and it has not worked well under certain circumstances and conditions.
I am also in favour of the resolution because it confers no special privileges and is not unfair to any province. If I thought it would help or would be partial to the province of Quebec, for example, 1 would be against it, or if I thought it would help the province of Ontario, I would be equally against it. I

believe that this resolution is the very bestway to rectify an anomaly in our present system of representation-I do not want to call it an injustice-and to bring about a fairer representation so far as the whole country is concerned.
Before I proceed any further I want to quote a statement by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), which in effect is endorsed by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low). Speaking on June 6, the leader of the C.C.F. party said, as reported in Hansard, page 2236.
But in fairness to other members of the house who agreed to deferring redistribution in 1941 I am not at this moment asking that another privilege of that kind be granted to western Canada. I believe that the proposal placed before the house by the government at 'the present time is fair, just, sound and constitutional.
Those are the words of a true Canadian. On a discussion of this kind it would be very easy indeed to arouse the passions even of members of parliament; very easy for them to speak in local or provincial terms. Those two hon. members did not do that. They may have some arguments against redistribution based on the census of .1941, as was so well expressed by the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) in 1943 when we asked for an amendment of the British North America Act, on account of the shifting of population from the western provinces to the Atlantic and the Pacific coasts and also to the two central provinces. It would have been easy for these hon. members to make a passionate appeal to their own people and demand that we take as a basis the census which is at present under way in the western provinces. They did not do that, and I want to praise them for their attitude on that score. It shows a real federal spirit.
As to the amendment brought in by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefen-baker) I am strongly against it. My views in this respect are influenced by section 52 of the British North America Act, which reads as follows:
The number of members of the House of Commons may be from time to time increased by the parliament of Canada, provided the proportionate representation of 'the provinces prescribed by this act is not thereby disturbed.
In this section is given to the federal representation all the authority and responsibility that could be required. I for one am not going to throw away the prerogatives of members of this parliament for a mess of pottage. I for one am going to take the full responsibility imposed on me in accepting the mandate to represent my people in the federal house. I for one will always deal with any

Redistribution
matter on which we have full jurisdiction, not in a local or regional way but in a truly national way, as was done by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, the hon. member for Peace River and several other hon. members during the discussion. If the amendment brought in by the Progressive Conservative opposition were adopted, it would simply stultify the federal prerogatives and shackle the activities derived from our national autonomy, and I for one would be the last to be a party to that. In this instance, as in many previous ones, we have the spectacle of the premier of Quebec talking of provincial autonomy and alleging centralization under the federal government. It is an old bugbear which has been worked time and time again, in many instances with absolutely no reason, and generally speaking the people of Canada are getting wise to that situation. In many instances these charges are simply political dodges, and are advanced so as to embarrass the central government, purely for partisan and political reasons. We have here all the safeguards needed for the preservation of political autonomy. As was so well stated by the Minister of Justice, the members of this house come from the different provinces of the Canadian confederation, and along with our great and overpowering loyalty so far as the nation is concerned, we are yet primarily what may be called municipalists. So far as I am concerned I have a great pride in living in my own little town of Cochrane, in northern Ontario. I am proud of it, and I will work and fight for it. We are also what may be called regionalists. I like the region in which I live; I like the section in which my constituency is located; I like northern Ontario and am loyal to it. I will fight its battles, I will participate in everything which is for its benefit. And then I am a provincialist. I am proud to belong to the great banner province of Ontario and to have fought, as I will continue to fight, some of its battles. I am proud of all the governments we have had with their headquarters in Toronto, and I am not averse to proclaiming that pride even in the federal field. But beyond all that I am, like other speakers whom I have mentioned, also a federalist. I believe that federation is what made this nation. It was found possible in times of hardship and turmoil for four provinces of Canada to get together and lay this wonderful foundation of Canadian confederation. Every member of this parliament is proud of confederation. I repeat, however, that there is no necessity for Mr. Duplessis to raise the old scarecrow of provincial autonomy or to charge that the dominion government wants to centralize everything.
For many years I have been a member of parliament, and whether Conservatives or Liberals were in power I never saw in the action of any of our governments any suggestion of overcentralization. I never heard from any member of parliament, no matter from what section of the country he came, any advocacy of [DOT] intensive centralization. There have always been within our constitution safeguards for the provinces and safeguards also for the national government. No federal member would dare to do anything which would tend to weaken or abolish those safeguards. I say these things with some feeling, because we have heard in the past and will probably hear again in the future that the central government is a great octopus which seeks to spread its tentacles into every section of our provincial life. That is not true, and it does not voice the opinions of the people of Canada as a whole. One might say that the best safeguard, as indicated in the present discussion of the redistribution bill, is that two parties in the House of Commons are ready and willing to surrender to the provinces some of the prerogatives which are given to the federal government by the constitution. That shows the spirit which animates on many occasions the federal representation, which at times will go as far as to throw away our own prerogatives.
There has also been an objection from some quarters that we should be very careful about an application to the British parliament for an amendment of the Canadian constitution. I am going to speak very briefly on a subject which is in the minds of a great majority of the Canadian people, and has been for many years. To some of them it is still puzzling why we should have to request the British parliament to amend our constitution. It is true that it is a British statute, but in the full sense of the word it is really a Canadian statute. No doubt the British people and the British government have long been surprised that we have not been able yet to find a formula which will enable us to become masters of our own destinies, of our own legislation. I say that it must be puzzling to our British friends, because we speak a good deal, and rightly, of our autonomy, more particularly since the statute of Westminster. Somewhere something is lacking; but it must be within the powers and the intelligence of our people to find the necessary formula.
Consider, for example, the state of our dominion-provincial relations. Looking into the last two or three dominion-provincial conferences, what do we find? What happened at the last one which was held in April of this
Redistribution

year? Seven provinces were willing and ready to come to an agreement with the federal government, but apparently the two central provinces did not find it possible to accept the agreement. Many Canadians asked themselves, "What is the principle that governs us in these matters? Is it not true that the majority of the provinces, if not a majority of the total population of the country, were willing and ready to agree with the central government? What then is the reason for the failure to come to an understanding? That is the question that must be settled." At the next dominion-provincial conference we must devise some means whereby agreements that are acceptable to the great majority of the provinces will be endorsed without the necessity of complete unanimity. What machinery will be adopted. I do not know, but surely that question calls for our earnest consideration. Will one province have the power to veto an agreement arrived at by the rest of the dominion, or will two provinces be able to brush that agreement aside, or on the other hand will the question at issue be decided on the basis of ratio of population represented by the indivdiual provinces? These are problems that we shall have to solve.
The moment this country finds a formula whereby it can request the British parliament to facilitate our dealing with our own constitution, it will, I believe, be an easy matter to bring this about, and I do not think there will be any objection on the part of the British parliament. But in the meantime any appeal that is made to the British parliament must come from the central authority here, because precedents have been established and judgment has been rendered in one case whereby it is not possible for any individual province on its own initiative to make such representations before the British parliament.
It is the view of many Canadians that we should move cautiously in making any change in our constitution such as I have suggested. Are we prepared now to set up a commission representing every section of the population for the purpose of considering the question of the Canadian constitution? There will be some reactions from minority groups. No doubt the rights pertaining to the French language will be protected, just as the rights with respect to education being left entirely in the hands of the provinces will be safeguarded; and this applies also to the question of a civil code so far as the province of Quebec is concerned.
My own belief is that we shall soon be ready to play the part of masters of our own destiny. I think it must be puzzling to the British gov-

ernment itself as to why it is that we in Canada have not yet reached that stage where we can really call ourselves our own masters in regard to the constitution. I remember hearing some years ago certain striking remarks made by the then member for Labelle, Mr. Bourassa, in a speech which he delivered on minority rights and appeals to the privy council and to the British parliament for amendments to the Canadian constitution. One statement that Mr. Bourassa made at that time has always remained vivid in my mind. Let me try to repeat, if not his exact words, at least the meaning he sought to convey. Speaking of minority rights he said:	We
know that at the foot of the British throne, before the privy council, the French Canadian people, generally speaking, will receive justice in an impartial way. But suppose some of the rights of those people were crushed by one ' particular province in the Canadian confederation. Do we in Canada expect that Great Britain would send troops to defend those rights?
At the time I realized the full import of the statement by the then member for Labelle. He meant that if it were not within our own competence to solve the question of minority rights we could never expect to have that problem solved in any physical sense by Great Britain. That, I believe, was a strong lesson to the Canadian people, and I have tried to learn it. As far as I am personally concerned, I hope that within a period of ten years at most we shall have an all-Canadian constitution and that that constitution in its spirit and application will consist of more than merely written words.
It has been well said in this debate-it was said at an earlier stage of the debate by the member for Rosetown-Biggar-that the great glory of the British constitution lies in the fact that it is unwritten. There is profound meaning in that statement. It means that in the heart and mind and soul of the British people the ideals of democracy, the ideals of justice, are ever uppermost. I believe that these wonderful qualities are just as strong in the Canadian people. Canadians are just as much imbued with them as the British.
I myself belong to the minority of French descent, but I have no fear of the future. I am acquainted with nearly every section of our population, and I can say that I have never suffered by reason of my racial affiliations or of my faith. In my section of northern Ontario that circumstance has never been thrown up to me. I know something also of my own native province; and I would leave this thought with hon. members. Observe any English-speaking person who has resided for a

R edistribution
number of years in the old province of Quebec and who returns to one of the English-speaking parts of the dominion, and you will notice that he carries with him evidence of some of the finest characteristics of that old province of Quebec because the people there are naturally fairminded and broadminded. In a word, they are naturally Canadian, just as the people in the other sections of our Canadian population are Canadian.
It is for' this reason that I say the time is almost ripe, if it is not here already, for the formation of a commission to deal primarily with the structure of our dominion-provincial relations and to study the question as to what should constitute a majority, so far as compromise is concerned, as to what should constitute a veto, and what should be the actually functioning of such relations. I believe that the Canadian people generally are thinking a great deal about what happened at the last dominion-provincial conference, and they feel that because seven provinces out of the nine were ready to come to an agreement, some action should have resulted from the conference. The question is left completely undecided.
I submit that we must put our own house in order before we can go to the British parliament and ask them to amend the British North America Act in order to provide us with a new Canadian constitution. I do not wish to elaborate this argument; I think I have said enough to convince my own compatriots that there is no reason for entertaining any fears for the future. Safeguards with respect to minority rights must of necessity spring from ourselves, from the fair-mindedness and the spirit of justice of the majority; for if those safeguards do not come from that source, we shall not find them anywhere. I believe we have it within ourselves to provide the solution. We all come from stocks that believe in the principles of democracy and justice-stocks from old France, from central Europe and from Britain, transplanted to this half of the north American continent-and I for one shall rejoice in the day that we are masters of our own constitution. I say that for the reason that in my opinion it is within ourselves, within our own ability, to deal with all matters of this sort in an impartial and Canadian way.
Before I conclude I wish to quote from an article that appeared in Saturday Night on June 8, 1946, entitled "Provincial Veto." The title of the article is illuminating. It may give a new angle to this question which may also prove illuminating. I quote:
Mr. Duplessis seems to us to have chosen a bad moment for the assertion of the right of the provinces to veto proposed amendments to the Canadian constitution. If the principle which he invokes is sound to-day it will still be sound next year, by which time a better occasion for raising it may have presented itself. For we have to note that numerous occasions for raising it have presented themselves in the past and have not been utilized, and that neglect has not prevented Mr. Duplessis from raising it now; so presumably one more neglect would not damage it for the future.
The reason why we think this is a bad moment for Mr. Duplessis is that by raising it now he is claiming for Ontario-which has just as much veto power as Quebec-the right to veto a proposal which adds eight parliamentary seats to Quebec and leaves Ontario unchanged. On Mr. Duplessis' principle the present proportions are just as much the perpetual right of Ontario, removable only with Ontario's consent, as the sixty-five seats of Quebec are the perpetual right of Quebec. (We do not ourselves regard either right as perpetual, but Mr. Duplessis does.)
The situation is very embarrassing for Mr. Drew. Either he goes along with Mr. Duplessis, in which case he maintains the right of Ontario to veto the amendment, and will scarcely dare to accept the responsibility of not vetoing it, or he splits with Mr. Duplessis and abandons a rather substantial part of that concept of provincial supremacy in which the two premiers have been in agreement for several years. Mr. Duplessis is in no such dilemma; he has no objection to the redistribution as redistribution, and all he asks is the right to say "O.K." But Mr. Drew cannot say "O.K." if he has a right to say "No." The redistribution takes away something which, if Mr. Duplessis is right, is the indisputable and irremovable property of Ontario, and no Ontario government, however devoted to Rep. by Pop. and however friendly to Quebec, would dare to toss away eight seats which are Ontario's indisputable and irremovable property, even if the retention of them can only be defended by throwing Rep. by Pop. into the discard and explaining (as the Globe and Mail's Ottawa correspondent explained the other day) that Quebec should not have the same proportional representation as Ontario because its people are too much addicted to voting in "a solid bloc.
If the last part of the statement, which is taken from the Globe and Mail, were applied it would not show the true Canadian spirit, the spirit of tolerance that I mentioned a moment ago. If we followed that principle it would mean that Saskatchewan, because it voted C.C.F. at the last federal election, should not have the representation to which she is entitled. It would also mean that because Nova Scotia voted almost solidly Liberal at the last federal election she should not have the representation to which she is entitled. That kind of attitude is not Canadian; it is not even good Canadian journalism. So far as I am concerned I shall highly resent any appeal to passion on the question of redistribution. I shall always resent that any so-called national paper should have the audacity to say to the rest of Canada that Quebec has
Redistribution

not the democratic right, the national right, the individual right, the personal right, to have the representation that she has, because during the last few years she happened to vote solidly Liberal. If the Globe and Mail correspondent knew the history of Quebec, he would also admit that years ago, and for a long period of time, that old province voted almost solidly Conservative. These are things we must keep in mind. This is no time to raise one section of the country against the other. It is not Canadianism; it is not conducive to the making of a Canadian nation. I know whereof I speak, sir, because I live in a section of the country which has a mixed population, and it is typical of the rest of Canada. It is typical of the fine city of Toronto. In Toronto they have tolerance too. There are right-thinking fair minded people there. Statements of this kind are not conducive to tolerance, and we do not want to hear them when we are dealing with a bill having to do with redistribution.
I am sometimes shocked at the attitude of the historical-no, it is not historical, because it is too new-Progressive Conservative party on matters of this kind. I do not understand their amendment, particularly when they are willing and ready to destroy the prerogative and initiative of the federal representation. Why do they do it? It is not even good politics. I cannot understand why they do it, particularly in view of the fact that at some time in the future they may be called upon to assume government responsibility. If that time comes they will be caught by their own motion; they will be caught by their own resolution; they will be hamstrung by their own action; they will be caught by the statements they have been making from time to time in trying to destroy the prerogative and the initiative of the national government, without adding anything to the rights of the provinces.
I hope the Canadian people are getting sick and tired of the bugbear, often put out in the form of political propaganda, that the federal government is trying to centralize more and more in this country. Why do they do it? The activities of our provincial, federal and municipal governments are well defined, particularly provincial and federal, in our constitution. Individually no federal member will ever agree to any government trying to infringe upon provincial activities or autonomy. There may be some borderline cases in which the central government must of necessity seek advice and cooperation from the provincial governments, but that does not apply in all cases, and certainly it does not

apply at the present time. These are things that are worth remembering in questions of this kind.
I am completely in favour of the resolution, for one simple reason, namely, that I am convinced in my own mind that it does not favour any one province or any particular section of our population, but it is fair because it follows the principle of representation by population; and no matter what the learned constitutionalist or the learned debater may say, or what anybody else may say, they cannot destroy the argument for the justice and the fairmindedness which is implied in representation by population, implemented in this resolution.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
First, I should like to congratulate the previous two speakers this afternoon on their' fine presentations. One can easily see what an advantage a lawyer has in this chamber. I am going to speak briefly as a layman because the motion before the house is one which directly affects my province.
Unless the present provisions of the British North America Act are changed, Saskatchewan will shortly see her representation in this chamber cut, and cut unfairly, from twenty-one to seventeen members. This group does not believe that such a loss can be justified. Originally the British .North America Act was meant to provide representation by population. However, in recent years, because of certain protective clauses, discrepancies have crept into the representation. Under the act, redistribution would unjustly deprive Saskatchewan of four members and Manitoba of three, and at the same time it would give Ontario eight extra members, to which, on a population basis, she is not entitled. Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Alberta would each receive one extra and Prince Edward Island two extra. In other words, the present provisions of the British North America Act do not give us representation by population. Therefore the members of the C.C.F. group would not be satisfied with redistribution under the act as it stands at present.
We think the resolution we are now discussing would help to rectify the situation. It would provide for fairer representation in the House of Commons. Nonetheless we also believe that the proposed amendment has certain shortcomings, and I should like to deal briefly with them. Before doing so, perhaps I should comment on the position of the Conservative party in this matter. So far, no speaker of that group has actually criticized the resolution. Rather in principle, they have argued that the Canadian parliament

Redistribution
has no right to ask for an amendment to the constitution without having previously secured the consent of the provinces. To me this attitude does not seem logical. Furthermore such a principle might actually be vicious. It might mean that one province could veto progressive legislation which would be to the great benefit of the other eight provinces. Certainly in the past, if I have read my history correctly, there have been numerous occasions when the federal government amended the constitution without the consent of all of the provinces. For instance, in 1915 Sir Robert Borden sponsored a constitutional amendment to increase the number of senators from western Canada. On that occasion Prince Edward Island objected; yet the amendment was proceeded with. Again in 1943, as has been pointed out, Quebec objected to an amendment on redistribution, but again the amendment was proceeded with. I think it is significant that in both cases the Conservative party took a completely different stand than from what they are taking to-day. On those occasions they voted to amend the constitution, despite the opposition and dissent of one province. It seems to me they are not being consistent. We believe the Canadian parliament alone must decide who shall represent the people at Ottawa. This is purely a federal matter. We can see no reason why parliament should first consult the provinces. Those who are opposing this resolution, whether it be directly or indirectly, intentionally or unintentionally may prevent some of the provinces of this nation from having their fair number of representatives in the House of Commons.
What are the shortcomings of the resolution? First, as the hon. member for North Battleford (Mr. Townley-Smith) has suggested, we believe that because of its size and wealth the northwest territories should have at least one specific representative. Second, the proposed amendment contains no reference whatever to a change in the other branch of government which was set up by the British North America Act, the Canadian Senate. In my opinion this is unfortunate, because there are even more glaring inequalities of representation in the Senate than in the House of Commons. For instance, in 1941 the three maritime provinces had an approximate population of 1,130,000 persons; and they have twenty-four senators. All western Canada, including the northwest territories, Yukon, British Columbia and the three prairie provinces, had an approximate population of 3,300,000 persons, or three times that of the maritimes, yet it also has only twenty-four senators. To be even more
specific, the province of New Brunswick, with an approximate population of 450,000, has ten (senators. The province of Saskatchewan, with about 900,000 people or double the number of New Brunswick, has only six senators. The resolution before the house to-day makes no provision for fairer senate representation. Apparently old inequalities in that body will be allowed to continue.
As hon. members know, this group has always favoured abolition of the senate. If and when a C.C.F. government is elected to power, one of the first questions with which it will deal will be such abolition. In the meantime, however, if the senate must be continued, we think it should be reformed. Such action has been talked about for many years but nothing has ever been done about it. I am told that as far back as 1891 the Liberal platform contained a plank called "senate reform". When are we to have this reform? I suggest that we should have it at once. The motion before us proposes to amend the British North America Act to rectify injustices in House of Commons representation. Why should it not also rectify injustices in Senate representation?
Aside from unjust representation there are a number of other serious shortcomings in the. Canadian Senate. Hon. members know those shortcomings probably better than I do, but I should like to take several minutes to run over them. In the first place, senators are appointed rather than elected. They are in no way responsible to the people. It i: conceivable that some senators might bs appointed not so much for their ability as for their past party service. I say that it is conceivable. Certainly it is a fact that in the past the senate has been a haven for exmembers of parliament, cabinet ministers, and ex-members of provincial governments.
