subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened *with the greatest interest and admiration to the magnificent constitutional study given this afternoon by the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett). I also commend the spirit of justice which inspired the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette); let us hope that a great majority of the members from his province will follow him. The hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) also made a practical and interesting contribution to the debate.
Every hon. member is familiar with the sections of the British North America Act dealing with redistribution. They are sections 51 and 52. I submit it is important that we first study the origin of the sections in order to distinguish between principles and procedure. The Quebec conference which led to

the adoption of the Quebec resolutions was held in October, 1864. At page 32 of annex IV of the report to the honourable the Speaker of the Senate of Canada by the parliamentary counsel of the senate, referring to the enactment of the British North America Act under the title, "The .Quebec Conference of 1864", I find the following:
Although the Quebec resolutions cannot, in my opinion, for reasons assigned and to be assigned, be accepted as the basis of the British North America Act, it does not follow that they, or the minutes of the conference or any available records of discussions thereat, are not quite material to the purposes of this report. What *was resolved at Quebec and what was afterwards resolved at London differed not much in principle, although it differed immensely in detail. That the union should be one of a federal character-that the legislative residuum should be in the central parliament-that parliament's power should be general and provincial powers local-that there should be an upper and a lower house-that there should be three districts in the confederation, each equally represented in the upper house-that the commons representation should be based upon population . . . was all easily settled.
It is important to note, for the benefit of the argument I intend to develop that what was resolved at Quebec, and afterwards at London, did not differ much in principle, although it differed immensely in detail, from the British North America Act itself. The Quebec resolutions dealing with representation in the House of Commons were numbered 17 to 22 inclusive, and also 25. I shall read them, as a basis for my argument:
17.	The basis of representation in the House of Commons shall be population, as determined by the official census every 10 years; and the number of members at first shall be 194, distributed as follows:
And then follows the distribution, which I need not quote. Then, they continue:
18.	Until the official census of 1871 has been made up, there shall be no change in the number of representatives from the several sections.
Provinces were called sections, in the Quebec resolutions. Then:
19.	Immediately after the completion of the census of 1871, and immediately after every decennial census thereafter, the representation from each section in the House of Commons shall be readjusted on the basis of population.
20.	For the purpose of such readjustments Lower Canada shall always be assigned 65 members, and each of the other sections shall at each readjustment . . .
And then follows the readjustment, as set out in section 51. Then:
21.	No reduction shall be made in the number
of members returned by any section, unless its population shall have decreased, relatively to the population of the whole union, to the extent of five per centum.	_	.
22.	In computing at each decennial period the number of members to which each section is entitled, no fractional parts shall be considered.

Redistribution
unless when exceeding one-half the number entitling to a member, in which ease a member shall be given for each such fractional part.
25. The number of members may at any time be increased by the general parliament, regard being had to the proportionate rights then existing.
It is our section 52 of the act. The London resolutions were approximately the same, except for some minor changes, and also for the fact that they were renumbered. We find that 17 became 18, and 18 became 19. Some inconsequential words were added. Then, 19 became 20, and 20, 21 and 22 were renumbered as 21, 22 and 23. In each instance the word province was substituted for the word section.
Let us compare the London resolutions dealing with representation and redistribution with the text of the British North America Act. We cannot find section 18 in the text of the act. I offer it as my opinion that it was the most important one regarding representation in the House of Commons. Resolution 18 contains the very principle of representation in the House of Commons. Although I have read it I shall read it again:
The basis of representation in the House of Commons shall be population as determined by the official census every 10 years.
Two things: First, basis of representation shall be population; and, second, as determined by the official census every 10 years. The other sections 19 to 24 inclusive are reproduced in the statute in their spirit if not in their form. They are sections 51 and 52. They do not deal with the principle of representation, but they deal with the procedure of redistribution.
It is of the utmost importance that we distinguish between principles and rules of procedure to implement those principles. The principle or basis of representation in the House of Commons is not expressly worded in the British North America Act; but it may be inferred from sections 51 and 52, especially if one refers to the Quebec and London resolutions. That is most probably why so many people have always felt that the basis of representation was the number of 65 members for Quebec. Even the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) the other day as reported at page 2229 of Hansard said, when dealing with section 20 of the Quebec resolutions :
For the purpose of such readjustment Lower Canada shall always be assigned 65 members.
Then he went on to say:
That was the basis upon which the provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick entered confederation.
It has not and never has been a basis. It is only a means of attaining the implementing
of the principle which is, and always has been, proportionate representation by provinces according to population.
This afternoon the hon. member for Stan-stead contradicted the hon. member for Lake Centre when he said that the basis of representation is population. If the number of 65 members for Quebec was the principle on which the fathers of confederation intended to base representation in this house, what, then, is the use of section 52 of the British North America Act, which reads as follows:
The number of members of the House of Commons may be from time to time increased by the parliament of Canada, provided the proportionate representation of the provinces prescribed by this act is not thereby disturbed.
Everyone will admit that the rules of interpretation of statutes require that a meaning be given to any section in any act. A section cannot have been enacted just for the purpose of putting words one after another. Section
51	already provide a mechanism which may bring about, and effectively brought about, an increase in the number of members when the population of provinces other than Quebec increase more rapidly than that of Quebec.
If paragraph 62 refers to the same occurrence it is useless, unless one concludes that because only the word "increase" is used, no decrease can be made if the population of Quebec grows more rapidly than that of the other provinces. Nobody has ever thought it could mean that, because, first, section 52 would contradict section 51; and moreover it would be in direct contradiction of the principle of proportionate representation by provinces according to population.
The only meaning we can give to section 52 is that not only is the figure 65 for Quebec not the basis of representation but it could even be increased without amending the constitution provided-and I quote from section 52:
. . . proportionate representation of the provinces prescribed by this act is not thereby disturbed.
I do not want and I do not think it is necessary to discuss that point at length. It may be that some other meaning can be given to section 52. But I sincerely wonder which one, if we follow the rules of interpretation. The least we can say is that the wording of section
52	emphasizes the principle of representation which has to be inferred from sections 51 and 52. If what I have tried to show is true, namely, that the principle or the basis of representation is "proportionate representation by provinces according to population" and that section 51 contains the rules of redistribution to put the principle into effect, the question
Redistribution

that comes to our mind is the following: Have the said rules been so interpreted or have they worked in such a manner that the principle of representation has been safeguarded? The answer is certainly no, and everybody admits it. A great injustice has been created by the actual interpretation and working out of the rules. One province has so benefited by the interpretation of one rule that eight of its representatives in this house should not be here because they represent nobody according to our principles of representation. Here we have a resolution that will bring us back to the application of the true spirit of confederation and that will give the same measure of justice to each province.
I was much surprised to hear the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) state in the house the other night as reported at page 2250 of Hansard:
It is a political bill. It is not in the interests of the constitution or of real parliamentary representation. It is a half-baked scheme that will lead to more disunity than anything else.
I wonder which is the more political, the bill or his speech. How would one characterize what he added as reported at page 2251 of Hansard:
You will not have in this country any longer one province the representatives of which will continue to urge all the things they have urged since the beginning of the session, small secondary matters which do not result in any effective legislation.
I resent deeply that last part of his speech. I contend that any member from any province may urge any measure in this democratic parliament. Even the hon. member for Broadview cannot be denied this right. We do not contest his right to expound his antediluvian ideas about the status of Canada; we only discuss his opinions.
I repeat that the interpretation given by a tribunal, which is not Canadian, to subsection 4 of section 51 of the British North America Act has implied the creation of a privilege for one province to the detriment of all the other provinces. The decision of the privy council has always been considered as binding, whatever may be the considered opinion of the hon. member for Stanstead. Subsection 4 must disappear if we want to reestablish the true principles of representation as set forth by the fathers of confederation. Not only that, but the number of 65 members laid down in 1867 for Quebec when confederation embraced only four provinces and when the population of Canada was very small, is not convenient any longer. As was said by Mr. Georges Henri Dagneau:
[Mr. Lesajse.l
(Translation):
In 1867 the extent of Canada's future development was surely not and could not have been fully realized. That is precisely why by and by, the precautions taken in 1867 in favour of Quebec became useless and, I would say, detrimental to that province. Mr. St. Laurent's argument regarding the injustice of the clause under which a province stands to lose one or more members because of events which have led to an increase in another province's population, seems irrefutable. Quebec's population increases so rapidly that the quotient rises steadily, with the result that certain provinces whose development is held up, for some reason or other, witness a decrease in their representation at Ottawa.
(Text):
As far as I am concerned I cannot conceive that the rules of representation should permit a decrease in the number of members in this house when the population of the nation increases.
The resolution that we are now studying offers the only means of returning to the real spirit of the constitution. Mr. Lorenzo Pare made one of the best comments I have read. I quote:
(Translation):
Canadians are attempting to repair a part of the democratic machine which has become warped through wear. They are trying to restore an essential right of free citizens, inasmuch as the time has come to restore to each the democratic authority to which he is entitled within our parliamentary institutions. At the same time they are trying to respect, according to the spirit of the constitution, a right of which the French-Canadian minority was deprived by the very letter of the constitution. Indeed, the object and the principle of the bill introduced J'esterday in the House of Commons by the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, is to restore the democratic function of our dominion parliament, by reinstating representation based on population.
(Text): It has been said that we should not base redistribution on the census of 1941, that it would be unfair and that any redistribution should be postponed until after the census of 1951. If in 1943 redistribution was postponed for special and serious reasons it cannot be said that the situation is the same to-day, and I feel most strongly that the fear of small changes in population since 1941, which changes have always occurred in any previous period of ten years, is no reason for delaying redistribution any longer. It is our duty to proceed not only to amend the rules of redistribution but also to proceed with the actual process of redistribution itself.
I say this because if the number of 65 members set for the province of Quebec was only a means of attaining the realization of the principle of the proportionate representation of population by provinces, the requirement that redistribution should be proceeded with after each census is part of the principle

Redistribution
itself. I have already read resolution. 18 of the London resolutions-resolution 17 of the Quebec resolutions-but I think it is important that I should read the resolution once more to emphasize that last point:
The basis of representation in the House of Commons shall be population, as determined by the official census every ten years.
Consequently, not only do I approve this resolution, but I ask that redistribution according to the new rules should be proceeded with as soon as the amendment to the constitution is approved by the British parliament.
An important amendment to the resolution we are studying has been introduced by the hon. member for Lake Centre. His amendment is to the effect that the provinces should be consulted on the expediency of amending section 51 and that no such amendment should be made unless a satisfactory agreement is reached at such consultations. His amendment is based on this claim, and I now quote what the hon. member for Lake Centre said, as reported at page 2228 of Hansard:
One of the most consequential provisions of this resolution is the proposal to amend section 51 without consultation with the provinces which will be affected.
I admit that it is a difficult and important matter, and that it should not be dealt with without due consideration. The question is, can a majority of this house ask for an amendment to the constitution without any consultation with or the concurrence of a majority or of all the provinces?
First, let me say that if we amend section 51 it will not create a precedent. Section 51 has been amended many times since confederation at the request of both houses of this parliament and never has there been consultation with the provinces. In an able speech delivered in this house and recorded in Hansard, at page 2239, the hon. member for Charlevoix-Sa'guenay (Mr. Dorion) proved that point beyond any possible doubt. I do not intend to repeat what he has already said, but let me remind the hon. members for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) and Peace River (Mr. Low) that I was astonished to hear their sudden solicitude for the province of Quebec; we could not but listen with scepticism to the warnings they addressed to us with pathetic voices. It is surprising, or is it surprising to hear them raise the point for the first time when the proposed resolution is necessary to correct an injustice. In 1943 two of the hon. members I just mentioned were in the house when an amendment was introduced to postpone redistribution, but they did not oppose it. Is this good faith? I will go so far as to say that the mere fact that they
take the stand they do convinces me that the present resolution should be adopted. However, I want to discuss for a few minutes the constitutionality of the proposed method of amending section 51.
Is the B.N.A. Act a contract, a treaty, a compact, a compromise, or a statute? That question has been the subject of lengthy and profound studies by constitutional lawyers, able professors and great statesmen in this country. I am not in a position to give a final word, but my opinion is that the B.N.A. Act is a statute based on an understanding which may be called a compact or a compromise between the two great races who were here, in Canada, in 1867.
At the time of confederation, neither Lower Canada nor Upper Canada was satisfied with the working of the system of union and they desired another constitution. Representatives of the province of Canada and of the maritime provinces met in Quebec and London, England, to establish a system of federation in which the rights of the dominion and the provinces would be divided and the rights of the minority would be protected.
The fathers of confederation, when they met at Quebec and afterwards in London, did not write the statute which is now our constitution. They passed resolutions which contained principles. In reality, they made a compromise between the two races, but they did not write the statute, which was in fact written by what I will call a third party. Our constitution is not even part of our own statutes. We have to make a distinction between the compact itself which was the work of the fathers of confederation and the statute adopted by the British parliament.
It is of the utmost importance that We distinguish between the spirit of the compact and the letter of the statute.
I have already tried, and I hope, succeeded, at the beginning of my remarks, to establish that the principle or basis of representation in this house is proportionate representation by provinces. I have already read section 18 of the London resolutions, and I am sure hon. members still have it in their minds.
The other resolutions and section 51 provide only for the mechanism set out at the time, in 1867, according to the then existing conditions, to arrive at the realization in fact of the principle which is part of the compact.
If the principle, the basis, of the compact is not recognized any longer because of an interpretation of the statute which is not ours, and because of a change in conditions which affects the expected result of the procedure, then I say that we must request a change in the
Redistribution

letter of the statute so that the letter of the statute is in accordance with the compact. Let me emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that in asking for the change in the statute as we are now doing, we are far from breaking the compact; on the contrary, we are preserving it. Not only is it the right of this house, but it is its duty to take all means to ensure the preservation of the compact. We cannot risk the refusal, not of one province, but of a provincial government or legislature, especially if that province has been privileged owing to a departure from the principles of the compact.
One may ask, who shall decide the issue? Where does the letter of the statute differ from the spirit of the compact? Who shall decide whether a proposed amendment to the constitution is on a question of principle or on a question of detail, on a material or on a subsidiary issue? Up to now, it has been up to this parliament. All the precedents that we have were "des cas d'espece." This time, it is once more "un cas d'espece."
In his speech last week, the hon. member for Lake Centre quoted Doctor Ollivier a3 follows: Hansard, page 2229:
.. .it is easy to understand the danger in which the province of Quebec stands if it lacks the right to take part in deliberations on the subject of our constitution.
I will answer that in his most remarkable book, " Problems of Canadian Sovereignty," and in his testimony before the committee of 1935 on the B.N.A. Act, Doctor Ollivier divides his proposed new constitution into provisions which, amongst others, could be amended without the consent of the provinces because they affect the federal government alone and others which may require the consent of one, of the majority or of all the provinces, as the case may be.
It is important to note that Doctor Ollivier was referring not to amendments as they have been made since confederation, but to an ideal method of amending the constitution upon which the dominion and the provinces were asked to agree. He was not by any means suggesting that when a certain method has been in use for many years it should be repudiated the moment that the issue is one of rendering justice and fair play to all the provinces.
As I have already said, all previous amendments in matters of representation were "des cas d'espece" which tended to lead us away from the principle agreed to at the time of confederation. Now that the time has arrived to reestablish the principle, should we raise any objection to the same method of amendment which has been followed in the past?
[Mi. Lesage.]
But I do not say that we should necessarily proceed in the future as we proceeded in the past. I approve the proposal made by the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay to set up a commission to study the procedure for amending the constitution. Moreover, we should have the right to amend our own constitution without suffering the humiliation of having to apply to London every time we want a change made.
I concur entirely in the words of the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville in his interesting speech on the present resolution, as reported at page 2249 at Hansard'.
Our country now has the right to proclaim to the world its complete sovereignty. It owes to itself, by reason of the reputation it has acquired, alike at home and in international councils, to have that document which characterizes most of the sovereignty and the independence of a nation-its own constitution.
Before I close my remarks, I want to answer the plea, addressed directly to members from the province of Quebec by the hon. member for Peace River. After having opposed the procedure set forth in the resolution, he asks us to join with him in approving the amendment of the hon. member for Lake Centre. He said, as reported at page 2256 of Hansard:
Members from the province of Quebec have an opportunity now to strike a blow for unity and good feeling amongst the people of this country.
Let me answer, respectfully but firmly, the leader of the Social Credit group, that we will not follow him. He is asking us to strike a blow for Canadian unity in striking a blow to our own rights. Of course, it would be very' easy to save Canadian unity if one of the two main racial groups who compose this nation would bow to all ihe wishes of the other. We have here a perfect case where Canadian unity will be preserved by applying the full measure of justice. The proposed resolution does not carry any disproportion of privilege to anyone. It gives a full measure of justice. That is the way of reaching Canadian unity, and I stand by it. The hon. member for Peace River asks us to abandon rights for the sake of Canadian unity. Did we not at all times make concessions for Canadian unity and were we not criticized by our own people, and especially by his own supporters in my province, for not having resisted with sufficient energy the requests of the majority?
I will ask the hon. member for Peace River to try to inspire his own party with the same desire for unity and sincere cooperation that has inspired the policy of the party to which I am proud to belong. There is no one in

Redistribution
this house who wants unity in Canada more than I do. Unity in this country is a great end to attain because of the very difficulties involved in giving to each and all an equal measure of justice. Let us hope that all together, with all our good will, we shall bend ourselves to this great task so that Canada will become an example of unity in the divided world of our time.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
For the few minutes left this afternoon I am pleased to give my opinion on the resolution which is before the house. First, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) on the brilliant speech he made this afternoon. I am sure that those who followed his remarks will consider that he gave one of the most logical interpretations, if not the most logical, of subsection 4 of section 51 of the British North America Act. I hope I shall be pardoned if I confine my remarks mostly to the effects of this resolution upon the maritime provinces.
I do not intend to deal with the resolution in general, but I shall try to point out how it will affect the three provinces by the sea. I may say at the outset that, in my opinion, if any section of Canada will be more adversely affected than others it will be the three maritime provinces. The maritimes are, as we all know, to-day only a very small section of this great dominion. We have not the importance that we had in the days of confederation. As a matter of fact, one great Canadian statesman said that we were just the rags and tatters of confederation. This, of course, we do not consider to be a fact. However, we sometimes feel that, in view of the treatment we receive, possibly there are others who hold the same opinion.
This question of confederation, which is one that gave our provinces at the time of confederation the greatest concern, has given us also great concern ever since. The strict application of the letter of confederation, as laid down in the British North America Act, has resulted in the representation of these three provinces being reduced materially from the days of confederation. I would point out that we are the only section of Canada which has really lost in representation.
As a matter of history, the province of New Brunswick in 1867 had a population of 250,000 and at that time we had fifteen members. In 1941, with a population of 453,000 we had, as we still have, ten members, a reduction of five members or one-third of our representation. The province of Nova Scotia in 1867 had a population of 364,000 and nineteen members.
In 1941 their population had increased, to
577,000	and they now have twelve members. Prince Edward Island, as hon. members know, had six members at confederation and to-day it has four.
The point I wish to make is this. While the population of New Brunswick has increased 80 per cent from the days of confederation, the representation of our province has decreased 33i per cent, despite the fact that these three provinces have sent people all over Canada to build up the great west. Possibly more than any other section of the Canadian pop ulation, the people of the maritimes have helped to build up the west and this great Canada of ours.
We have protested on two different occasions against the reduction in our representation. The hon. member for Stanstead this afternoon cited the case of Prince Edward Island's representation before the supreme court of Canada and the judicial committee of the privy council. We thought that we had good grounds, that we had solid arguments. I am not going to repeat them here but the fact remains that we lost out in those courts. We are not finding fault to-day with this decision. The question of representation, as I say, was decided by the courts of the country, by the supreme court of Canada and by the judicial committee of the privy council. The letter of the law possibly was correct, but we feel that the spirit of the constitution, as represented at the time of confederation, was not carried out. The decision was made on the status, not the intention of the parties, and we are satisfied that it was not intended by those who drafted the British North America Act in 1867.
Quebec was selected as the unit, not because, as someone stated here, it had the largest population, but because the variations in that province would possibly be less than in any other province At that time, however, it was not anticipated that there would be a great increase in the territory of Quebec. The Quebec of to-day is not the Quebec of the days of confederation. Quebec has increased greatly in her territory and the unit of representation so far as Canada is concerned has been greatly increased. As I say, it was never anticipated that there would be such an increase in the unit of representation that the smaller provinces would have their original representation reduced.
I should like to read a quotation which was given by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), the other day. It consists of a statement made by the Hon. George
Redistribution

Brown at the time of confederation when he introduced a resolution with respect to representation. He said:
The practical result will be that while Lower Canada certainly will not be less-
I would point out that it has not been less. Quebec has had sixty-five members from the days of confederation; she has sixty-five to-day. I continue with the quotation:
-and the lower provinces may increase in population, they cannot decrease in the number of representatives.
That was the intention of the act at that time, whether it was the letter of the act or not.
I should also like to quote what Sir Alexander Galt said three years before confederation when the terms were being considered. He said:
We have supposed that the population of Lower Canada being tolerably equable in its character, would afford the best basis. But having respect to the rapid increase of Upper Canada, we think the lower provinces should not be reduced if they do not increase in the same ratio. Therefore the lower provinces would have the same as they have now-unless in the very improbable case of any one falling off by five per cent or more.
I would point out that both these men did not anticipate that there would be a decrease, or such a decrease in the representation of the maritime provinces. We have heard this afternoon an explanation of why this five per cent was put in the act. We have heard other statements that it was doubtful just why it was put there. If hon. members would read the history of confederation they would come to the conclusion that five per cent was put in the act to protect the maritime provinces. I confess that it has not acted in that way. These men did not have the vision or possibly the foresight. It has reacted to the benefit of the great province of Ontario, but it has never reacted in any way to the benefit of the three maritime provinces.
I am also satisfied that had the two provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, which formed two of the great pillars of this confederation and to which this country owes possibly more than is realized by many hon. members here, known that their representation was to be reduced even to what it is to-day I do not believe that they would have joined confederation, and I do not believe that there would be any Canada to-day. We lost all along the line. We lost our trade. Before confederation, the maritime provinces were perhaps the most progressive and the most prosperous parts of the British part of North America. We traded with the New England states; our ports were busy; our farmers

received good prices and markets for all that they produced. This was all lost after confederation. We lost our manufacturers. Every small city and town in the maritimes had its manufacturing interests. After confederation, they all moved to Quebec or Ontario. We have now lost our representation and our United States trade.
When I was in London a little over a year ago I had the honour and the pleasure of visiting Sir Andrew Rae Duncan, who, as hon. members will remember, wrote the Duncan report on the rights of the maritime provinces. He asked me what part of Canada I came from. I said: "I come from the province of New Brunswick." He said: "Well, there is only one thing I can say about you people in the maritime provinces. You are the most long-suffering people that are to be found most anywhere in t'he world." He told me that the Duncan report had never been implemented; that we had in no way received from the rest of Canada the rights to which we were entitled, and which he recommended.
After confederation, we expected our province to increase in population. For instance, Saint John was told that it would be the Liverpool of America. Anyone can go to Saint John to-day and see how the trade of that port has decreased, except in war time. I might also point out that before confederation Saint John was the fourth largest shipping port in the world.
A few moments ago I mentioned that the yardstick of representation had been increased. I would point out that in 18118 100,000 square miles were added to Quebec. In 1012 another
400,000	square miles were added to that province. The unit of measurement became completely out of line.
There has been an increase in population in other provinces out of proportion to the maritime provinces, because not only did Quebec receive a great increase in territory, but Ontario was greatly increased. All this northern country, these great rich mines which Ontario and Quebec have to-day, were given out of the realm of this country which belonged as much to the maritime provinces as it did to any other part of Canada. They purchased from the Hudson's Bay company great stretches of territory. This territory was purchased with money belonging to the people of the maritime provinces and from other parts of Canada. We in the maritimes cannot increase in area; we are circumscribed by the sea. The little province of Prince Edward Island is an island. There is no possibility of its increasing its territory. Nova Scotia is almost completely an island. She cannot increase in area. New Brunswick

R edistribution
could not increase in area unless we took a part of Quebec. If we took part of Quebec we would have to take over the constituency of Temiscouata, and as everyone knows that would only be borrowing trouble for New Brunswick, much as we would feel honoured by having the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) a representative of the province.
Some people think our provinces are not densely populated, but to show the house that we have the most densely concentrated population in Canada I shall read from the Canada Year Book of 1941, which shows that in that year the number of persons per square mile was as follows: Prince Edward Island, 43.52, the highest in Canada; Nova Scotia, 27.86; New Brunswick, 16.65; Quebec, 6.36; Ontario, 10.43; Manitoba, 3.32; Saskatchewan, 3.77; Alberta, 3.20 and British Columbia, 2.28. From these figures it will be seen that while the population of our provinces has in no way reached the saturation point, yet we have far more people to the square mile than has any other part of Canada. There is no possibility of increasing our territory and we cannot hope for a greater population-because, as I say, we are the most densely populated part of Canada to-day. They speak about representation by population. That sounds very good, but I should like to ask when we have ever had in fact representation by population in this country. If hon. members will read the history of Canada they will find that such has not been the case. For instance, when Manitoba came into confederation in 1870, according to her population and taking Quebec as the yardstick she was entitled to only one member, but she was given four. In other words, her representation was four times that to which she was entitled. In 1881 she was entitled to three members and was given five. In 1873 Prince Edward Island was entitled to five members and was given six. At confederation British Columbia was entitled to two members and was given six.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
My understanding is that British Columbia refused to come into confederation unless she was guaranteed six members; and if the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) will look up the records I think he will find that to be the fact. In 1881, quite a number of years after British Columbia came in, she was entitled to only two members, but she still had six.
I mention these facts to show that while we speak about representation by population, that theory has never been followed in this dominion. Population has never been the exclusive yardstick.
We may be told that the maritime provinces are given special consideration under the provisions of this resolution. We have had those special provisions since 1914. Nothing new is being given the maritime provinces; as a matter of fact, if we analyse it, something is being taken away In 1914, I think it was, Mr. E. N. Rhodes was responsible for the inclusion, in the petition then being sent to Westminster, for the following:
Notwithstanding anything in this section, if upon completion of a computation under rules one - and two, the number of members to be assigned to a province is less than the number of senators representing the said province, rules one and two shall cease to apply in respect of the said province, and there shall be assigned to the said province a number of members equal to the said number of senators.
This principle, though perhaps not in those words, was enunciated by Mr. Rhodes, and he was responsible for the consequent amendment at that time. As I tried to point out a few moments ago, we do not consider our representation fair and adequate in view of the importance of our three provinces. In the first place, they are important from a geographical point of view. I ask hon. members to think what Canada would be without the maritime provinces. We have just passed through a great war, during which the great port of Halifax in the maritime provinces played a part as important as that played by any port in the British empire or possibly any of the allied nations. I have seen from a hundred to a hundred and fifty ships lined up in Bedford basin carrying food, munitions and soldiers. Our soldiers fought a great fight, but the port of Halifax played a great part in preserving liberty not only in this country but throughout the world. I could point also to the contribution made by the city of Saint John in the same way, and to many other contributions we have made of our resources, which were handed over to the dominion at the time of confederation. It is not necessary for me to go into details; I am sure if hon. members will stop and think for a moment they will realize the great importance of the maritime provinces. During the winter, when the great ports of Montreal and Quebec are sealed with ice, the trade of this country depends upon Saint John and Halifax.	.
It may be said that this is not the pact of confederation. Well, I would point out that as far as this pact is concerned the letter of
Redistribution

the bond has not been observed in the past. On that point I should like to quote a gentleman who left this house not long ago, who I consider was one of the great members of this parliament in recent years. I refer to Hon. Mr. Ralston, who in 1933, at page 5519 of Hansard for that year, referring to the British North America Act said:
The letter of the bond has not been observed and nobody has insisted upon it being observed in the matter of relief. The letter of the bond was not observed in the matter of the return of the natural resources which were the property of the dominion. The letter of the bond has not been observed with regard to the extraordinary efforts which have had to be made in order that our people may be clothed and fed and in order that the emergent conditions in which we find ourselves may be met.
Our provinces have always felt that if the spirit of the British North America Act had been carried out, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia would have the same number of members to-day that we had at the time of confederation. Australia, possibly bearing in mind what happened in Canada, took care to see that the smaller states were not affected in this way when that country was united into one great commonwealth. Of the 75 members in their house one state had 26, another had 23, another 9, another 7, and two others 5 each. Their act contained express provision that none of these states should have fewer members than it had at the time of the union, and that provision has been carried out. In 1907, when Mr. Hughes of Prince Edward Island brought up in the House of Commons this matter of representation, many of the leaders of that time, including Sir Robert Borden, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and others, spoke on the question. The hon. member for Lake Centre has placed on Hansard many of the opinions expressed on that occasion by these great statesmen. At page 2202 of Hansard for 1907 Sir Robert Borden said:
I am inclined to think that the larger provinces would answer a question of that kind very much in the spirit which the Prime Minister himself has expressed and would be inclined to give the three maritime provinces, whose population has not increased so rapidly as that of other parts of the dominion, representation which should never be smaller than at the time when those provinces entered confederation.
Instead of the same representation, as I say, our representation is growing smaller as time goes on.
In 1907 Sir Wilfrid Laurier spoke in the same debate, and discussed the question brought up by the 'hon. member for Lake Centre, a question which is of vital importance to hon. members from the maritime provinces. I believe it is more vital to us than to the
fMr. Brooks.]
people in any other section in Canada. We stand to lose the most. I hope every member from the maritimes, be he Liberal or Progressive Conservative, will support that which I believe will be in the best interests of our three provinces.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT AS TO RULES FOR READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
I should like to quote the words of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, as they were expressed in 1907:
Confederation is a compact, made originally by four provinces, but adhered to by all the nine provinces, who have entered it, and I submit to the judgment of this house and to the best consideration of its members, that this compact should not be lightly altered. It should be altered only for adequate cause, and after the provinces themselves have had an opportunity to pass judgment on the same.
That was a leader of the party opposite. No one, least of all, I am sure, the hon. member for York-Sunbury, will question the Canadianism of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. He continued by saying:
My hon. friend from York, N.B. (Mr. Crocket), stated in the course of his argument that we have announced in the speech from the throne that we are going to ask parliament to alter the financial terms of confederation. That is very true; but my hon. friend should know that we did not come to that conclusion except after conference with the provinces and after all the provincial governments had united in a prayer for the same.

Right Hon. C. D. Howe
That was on a financial matter; and I would say that representation of the people is of far greater importance than a matter of finance.
Then, speaking on the same day and in the same debate Sir Robert Borden said this, as reported at page 2200 of Hansard:
I agree with what has been said by the right hon. gentleman regarding the undesirability of lightly amending the terms of our constitution and am inclined to agree with him on the necessity of some consultation with the provinces, although of course all the provinces are represented here. But inasmuch as this is a federal compact which we are asked to vary, it is only right that each province should be consulted and its decision given, in the right of its separate entity. But I am not inclined to agree altogether in some of the suggestions urged by my hon. friend.
I could go on quoting the words of leading statesmen and, as my good friend the hon. member for Stanstead has said, from the words of the best constitutional lawyers this country has ever produced. One could quote from them all where they have said that in a matter of this kind the provinces should be consulted.
I hold in my hand a quotation from the words of E. M. Macdonald, who at one time was a representative of Pictou in this chamber. At page 2186 of Hansard of the same year, 1907, he stated most emphatically that in a matter of this kind the provinces should be consulted. If my memory serves me correctly, E. M. Macdonald was one of the leading Liberals from that province.
We do not fear so much some of the older provinces in the dominion. We do not fear Quebec; she has been our neighbour since confederation, and I think no one will say that the maritime provinces and Quebec have not got along well together. We feel, so far as that old province is concerned, that with their generous nature we shall be used properly.
We do not fear the old province of Ontario which, too, was one of the cornerstones of confederation. The history of that province is old, like that of the maritimes and Quebec.
So far as the west is concerned, one might say they are new. Possibly they do not have the same ideals as the older provinces have. Those provinces have been populated with people from all parts of the world, to a greater extent than in the other provinces. The ancestors of the families in these older provinces came to them 300 or 400 years ago. But in the western provinces-and I have no criticism in this regard-many of their people came from different sections of Europe. They filled western Canada, and I do not believe
they understand fully the history and traditions of Canada, as do the people in the older provinces.
I am reminded of this when I hear statements such as those made this afternoon by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) who said that when or if the C.C.F. party comes into power, the first thing they would do would be either to abolish or reform the senate. What would it mean to the protection of the maritime provinces, with the section in the act as it now is, if the senate of this country were abolished? What protection would we have?
It is for reasons such as this, that I appeal to the house not lightly to allow a change in the act so that, if by any chance-and God forbid that it should happen-a C.C.F. government should take office, with their ideas of reforms, the old traditions and customs might be preserved.
